analysis.one_liner: Blocks IRS rules that would close valuation discounts used to shrink estate tax bills.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee on September 15, 2016 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: In August 2016 the IRS proposed rules under tax code section 2704 that would limit 'valuation discounts' — accounting techniques that let families knock down the taxable value of business interests they pass to heirs, shrinking estate and gift tax bills. This bill would make those rules, and any similar future ones, legally void. It never moved past committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Very wealthy families that hold businesses through family partnerships and LLCs and use valuation discounts to reduce estate and gift taxes when transferring wealth to the next generation. Estate-planning lawyers and wealth advisors who build those arrangements also keep their business model intact.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would strip the August 4, 2016 proposed section 2704 regulations, and any substantially similar future regulations, of all force or effect [S2][S3].
Those regulations would restrict discounts that reduce the taxable value of interests in family-owned entities for estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer tax purposes [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Federal revenue. Rules that curb valuation discounts would increase estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer tax paid on large family wealth transfers, so voiding them forgoes that revenue and shifts more of the general tax burden onto everyone else.
analysis.who_pays_short: The federal treasury and ordinary taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Nullifying the regulations would permanently preserve estate-tax valuation discounts, reducing the tax paid when the largest family fortunes transfer between generations [S2][S3].
Forfeited estate and gift tax revenue must be replaced by other taxes, borrowing, or spending cuts, which fall on the broader public.
Override by statute of a specific proposed rule, including any 'substantially similar' future attempt, ties the IRS's hands on valuation policy regardless of future evidence [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit goes almost entirely to households wealthy enough to owe estate or gift tax — only estates over the exemption threshold, worth millions per couple, use these discounts. The cost is forgone federal revenue. For ordinary working people there is no direct benefit and a modest indirect cost through the tax base.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017 [S1][S5].

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 15, 2016 and referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day [S1][S5].
No further action was ever taken; the committee reported nothing, and the bill never reached the House floor [S5].
Because the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, an unreported bill dies automatically and would have to be reintroduced from scratch in the next Congress [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: With no vote ever held, the proposed section 2704 rules were never nullified by Congress, so the Treasury retained the legal option to curb estate-tax valuation discounts — the general taxpayer came out ahead relative to what this bill would have done.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers; the bill died in committee

for.name: Rep. F. James Sensenbrenner Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to nullify the IRS section 2704 proposed regulations.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Kevin Brady)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill sat without action from referral until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so no recorded opposition exists; the only recorded support was two Republicans (the sponsor and one cosponsor) [S4].

industries.industry: Wealthy family business owners and family limited partnerships
industries.note: Blocking the section 2704 rules preserves valuation discounts that shrink estate and gift taxes on multi-million-dollar family wealth transfers, costing the federal treasury revenue that others ultimately make up.
Nullifying the rules keeps the discount-based planning techniques — a core fee-generating service — fully usable, at the cost of tax revenue that would otherwise come from their clients' estates.
The bill voids the agency's proposed rules and bars any substantially similar attempt, removing a tool for collecting transfer taxes on the largest estates.
